title: Setting up word problems
blurb: Read the question first, pick the right model, keep units consistent and answer the exact question asked, not a step along the way.
question: A 750 mL IV bag is hung. The nurse infuses 2/5 of it before noon, then 1/3 of what remains during the afternoon. The TEAS asks how much is left in the bag, and one of the options is the amount left at noon. How do you set up a multi-step word problem so you answer the question actually asked?

teach.h: Word problems are reading problems first
teach.body: Formally, a word problem describes a real situation that you model with operations, an expression, an equation or an inequality, and then solve. In plain English: most wrong answers on TEAS word problems are not arithmetic mistakes, they are answering the wrong question. The options are built from the numbers you would get one step early, with mixed units or with a total when a difference was asked. A fixed routine protects you.

steps.label: Read the last line
steps.sub: What exactly is asked? In what units?

steps.label: Estimate
steps.sub: Roughly how big should it be?

steps.label: Compute
steps.sub: One step at a time; round at the end

steps.label: Check
steps.sub: Units, size, and the question asked

teach.h: Answer the question, not a step
teach.body: Underline the question before you start: 'how much is LEFT', 'how many MORE', 'what is the TOTAL', 'how many FULL doses'. Then keep that in view while you work, because every intermediate value is likely to be an option. 'How many more' always ends with a subtraction. 'How much is left' ends with what remains, not what was used. 'How many containers' ends with rounding up; 'how many full doses' ends with rounding down.

teach.h: Common problem families and their models
head: Family
Model
Example

items: Question: how much is LEFT in the 750 mL bag at the end?
Before noon: 2/5 of 750 = 750 × 2 ÷ 5 = 300 mL used. Left: 750 − 300 = 450 mL.
Afternoon: 1/3 of the REMAINDER (450, not 750) = 150 mL used. Left: 450 − 150 = 300 mL.
Distractors you would see: 450 mL (left at noon, one step early) and 200 mL (the afternoon 1/3 taken from the full 750 instead of the remainder).

teach.text: The four costliest slips: stopping one step early, answering 'how many more' with a total, mixing units (minutes with hours, mL with L, cents with dollars), and doing elapsed time as decimal subtraction. 9:15 − 6:50 is not 2.65; it is 2 hours 25 minutes. And 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes, not 1 hour 50 minutes.

items: From 2:45 p.m. to 5:10 p.m.: count up in friendly chunks. 2:45 → 3:00 is 15 min; 3:00 → 5:00 is 2 h; 5:00 → 5:10 is 10 min.
Total: 2 h + 15 min + 10 min = 2 h 25 min. Check: 2:45 + 2 h 25 min = 4:70 = 5:10. ✓
24-hour (military) time: for 1300 to 2359, subtract 12 hours for p.m. 1430 = 2:30 p.m.; 2145 = 9:45 p.m.; 0000 = midnight; 1200 = noon.
Decimal hours to minutes: multiply the decimal part by 60. 2.4 h = 2 h + 0.4 × 60 min = 2 h 24 min.

teach.h: Counting up from 2:45 p.m. to 5:10 p.m.

items: Jamal, a nursing applicant, takes home $1,840 a month. Rent is $725, his car costs $260 and groceries $310. He saves 15% of his take-home pay. How much is left for everything else?
Savings first (15% of take-home): 0.15 × 1,840 = 276. Check: 10% is 184 and 5% is 92; 184 + 92 = 276. ✓

children.label: Operations in order
children.sub: work step by step; answer the last step

items: Read the last line first and underline exactly what is asked, with its units.
Convert everything to one unit before computing.
Elapsed time: count up in chunks; never subtract times as decimals.
Round only at the end, and in the direction the context needs.
Check the answer against the question: left vs used, more vs total, full doses vs containers.

summary: You can now work any TEAS word problem with a fixed routine: identify exactly what is asked, list facts in consistent units, choose an operation, equation or inequality model, and check the answer against the question. You can also handle elapsed time, 24-hour times and decimal hours without slipping.

A.q: A nursing shift report began at 6:50 a.m. and ended at 9:15 a.m. How long did the report last?
A.why: Count up: 6:50 → 7:00 is 10 min; 7:00 → 9:00 is 2 h; 9:00 → 9:15 is 15 min. Total: 2 h 25 min.

whyNot.0: 3 h 25 min subtracts the minutes (50 − 15 = 35, so 60 − 35 = 25) but forgets to borrow the hour.
whyNot.2: 2 h 65 min subtracts the times as decimals (9.15 − 6.50); an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
whyNot.3: 3 h 35 min counts 6:50 to 9:50 as 3 hours and then adds the extra 35 minutes instead of taking them off.

A.q: A 1,200 mL bag is hung. In the morning, 3/8 of it is infused. In the afternoon, 1/2 of what remains is infused. How much is left in the bag?
A.why: Morning: 3/8 × 1,200 = 450 mL used, leaving 750. Afternoon: 1/2 × 750 = 375 used, leaving 375 mL. Check: 450 + 375 + 375 = 1,200. ✓

whyNot.0: 750 mL is what was left after the morning, one step early.
whyNot.1: 150 mL takes the afternoon half from the full 1,200 instead of from the remainder.
whyNot.2: 825 mL is the total infused (450 + 375), not the amount left.

A.q: An electrician charges a $90 service fee plus $62 per hour. The bill was $400. How many hours did the electrician work? Round to the nearest tenth if needed.

whyNot.1: 6.5 hours divides the whole bill by the hourly rate and ignores the service fee.
whyNot.2: 7.9 hours adds the fee instead of subtracting it: 490 ÷ 62.
whyNot.3: 3.4 hours divides by the service fee instead of the hourly rate: 310 ÷ 90.

B.q: During a shift, a patient drank 1.2 L of water, 350 mL of juice, 0.25 L of milk and 480 mL of tea. What was the total intake in milliliters?

whyNot.0: 831.45 adds liters and milliliters as if they were the same unit.
whyNot.1: 2,055 mL converts 0.25 L to 25 mL; it is 250 mL.
whyNot.3: 4,530 mL converts 0.25 L to 2,500 mL; it is 250 mL.

B.q: Clinic A vaccinated 1,245 patients in March and 1,580 in April. Clinic B vaccinated 2,915 patients over the same two months. How many more patients did Clinic B vaccinate than Clinic A?

whyNot.1: 335 is how many more Clinic A vaccinated in April than in March.
whyNot.2: 2,825 is Clinic A's total, one step short of the difference.
whyNot.3: 5,740 adds both clinics' totals; 'how many more' needs a subtraction.

B.q: Phone plan A costs $30 a month plus $0.10 per text. Plan B costs $45 a month with unlimited texts. For how many texts in a month do the two plans cost the same?

whyNot.0: 15 is the dollar difference between the plans, not the number of texts.
whyNot.1: 450 divides Plan B's whole price by $0.10 and ignores Plan A's $30 base.
whyNot.2: 750 adds the two monthly prices (75 ÷ 0.10) instead of finding their difference.

C.q: A bottle holds 240 mL of an oral medication. Each dose is 7.5 mL, given 3 times a day. For how many FULL days will the bottle last?
C.why: Per day: 7.5 × 3 = 22.5 mL. 240 ÷ 22.5 = 10.67 days. Only full days count, so 10. Check: 10 days use 225 mL; an 11th day would need 247.5 mL.

whyNot.0: 32 is the number of single doses (240 ÷ 7.5), not days.
whyNot.1: 11 rounds 10.67 up, but there is not enough medication for an 11th full day.
whyNot.3: 10.7 is not a whole number of days; the question asks for full days.

C.q: Jada earns $19.50 an hour and works 36 hours a week. Her employer withholds 20% of her pay. She spends $310 a week. How much does she have left to save each week?

whyNot.0: $392.00 subtracts spending from gross pay and forgets the 20% withholding.
whyNot.1: $313.60 takes 20% off after subtracting spending; withholding comes out of the full paycheck.
whyNot.3: $140.40 is the amount withheld (20% of 702), not the amount left.

C.q: A clinic uses 5 gallons of distilled water a week. Water is sold in 1.5-liter bottles. Using 1 gallon = 3.785 liters, how many bottles must the clinic buy each week?
C.why: 5 × 3.785 = 18.925 L. 18.925 ÷ 1.5 = 12.6 bottles. To have enough, round up: 13 bottles.

whyNot.0: 12 bottles hold 18 L, short of the 18.925 L needed; 'enough' means round up.
whyNot.1: 4 divides 5 gallons by 1.5 liters without converting units.

reteach.title: A GPS for word problems
reteach.question: A GPS asks for your destination before it plans the route. What happens if you start driving before you know where you are going, and how does that match a word problem?

blocks.body: A GPS never starts with the first turn; it starts with the destination. In a word problem the destination is the question's last line: 'how much is LEFT', 'how many MORE', 'how many FULL doses'. Each calculation is a turn along the route. The distractors are the places you pass on the way: the remainder after one step, the amount used, the total before the subtraction. Arrive at the destination, not at a stop along the way.

blocks.h: The IV bag route: destination 'how much is left'

steps.sub: 450 left: a stop, not the end

blocks.text: If your answer appears among the options after only one step of a multi-step problem, be suspicious. Reread the last line before you choose.

explain.body: Read the last line first. 'How many more' ends with a subtraction from a goal or another total. Convert hours and minutes to decimal hours properly: 45 minutes = 0.75 hour.

test.q: Bianca studied 2.5 hours on Monday, 1 hour 45 minutes on Tuesday and 3 hours on Wednesday. Her goal was 9 hours over the three days. How many more hours does she need?
test.why: 1 hour 45 minutes = 1.75 hours. Studied: 2.5 + 1.75 + 3 = 7.25. Still needed: 9 − 7.25 = 1.75 hours.

whyNot.1: 7.25 hours is how much she has studied, not how much more she needs.
whyNot.2: 2.05 hours writes 1 hour 45 minutes as 1.45 hours; 45 minutes is 0.75 hour.
whyNot.3: 16.25 hours adds the goal to the hours studied instead of subtracting.

explain.body: To turn a decimal part of an hour into minutes, multiply it by 60. 2.4 hours = 2 hours + 0.4 × 60 = 2 hours 24 minutes.

test.q: A procedure is scheduled to take 2.4 hours and starts at 9:30 a.m. At what time should it end?

whyNot.0: 12:10 p.m. reads 2.4 hours as 2 hours 40 minutes.
whyNot.2: 11:34 a.m. reads 2.4 hours as 2 hours 4 minutes.
whyNot.3: 11:24 a.m. adds 2 h 24 min to 9:00 and drops the 30 minutes.

explain.body: Write total = fixed + rate × quantity, then solve: subtract the fixed fee, then divide by the rate.

test.q: A taxi charges $3.25 plus $2.40 per mile. A ride cost $27.25. How many miles was the ride? Round to the nearest tenth if needed.

whyNot.0: 11.4 miles divides the whole fare by $2.40 and ignores the $3.25 fixed charge.
whyNot.2: 12.7 miles adds the fixed charge instead of subtracting it: 30.50 ÷ 2.40.
whyNot.3: 7.4 miles divides by the fixed charge instead of the per-mile rate: 24 ÷ 3.25.

explain.body: When you need enough containers, vehicles or packs, round UP even if the decimal is small. When only complete doses or items count, round DOWN.

test.q: A van seats 14 passengers. 75 nursing students need rides to a clinical site at the same time. How many vans are needed?
test.why: 75 ÷ 14 = 5.36. Five vans carry only 70 students, so round up: 6 vans.

whyNot.0: 5 vans seat 70 students, leaving 5 without a ride.
whyNot.2: 5.4 is not a whole number of vans; the answer must be interpreted in context.
whyNot.3: 61 subtracts one van's seats from the number of students instead of dividing.
